stories.headline: Sources: Pacers' Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) to miss time
stories.summary: Pacers star Tyrese Haliburton has a strained left hamstring and will miss time, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.
stories.body:
Indiana Pacers star Tyrese Haliburton has a strained left hamstring and will miss time, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Wednesday.

How long Haliburton will be sidelined is currently unclear, as Pacers team doctors and Haliburton are still gathering a clear timeline for his recovery, sources told ESPN.

Haliburton played in the first four games of the season for Indiana -- including a back-to-back this past Sunday and Monday -- after he had missed 16 months while recovering from a torn Achilles suffered in the 2025 NBA Finals.

He acknowledged feeling "a little beat up" after Monday's game in Milwaukee before appearing on the injury report Wednesday.

Haliburton had been averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds on 52% shooting while playing 33 minutes per game to start the season.

Haliburton becomes the latest in an influx of star players sidelined with injuries to start the season, including Oklahoma City's Jalen Williams, Minnesota's Anthony Edwards and Toronto's Kawhi Leonard.

Injuries are also already beginning to pile up for Indiana, who had four of their five starters appear on the injury report for Wednesday's game against the Philadelphia 76ers.

Ivica Zubac was already ruled out Wednesday's game with a left ankle sprain, while T.J. McConnell has a right hamstring strain and has yet to play this season. Ben Sheppard tore his left meniscus, and Johnny Furphy had surgery on his right ACL.

Andrew Nembhard missed Monday's game in Milwaukee and is also listed as questionable heading into Wednesday's game with neck soreness.

The Pacers won 19 games, the fewest wins in a season in franchise history, while Haliburton was sidelined for the entire 2025-26 season.

stories.headline: Man United's Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes hold 'clear-the-air' talks - reports
stories.summary: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have held clear-the-air talks.
stories.body:
Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick and captain Bruno Fernandes have held clear-the-air talks, according to multiple reports Wednesday.

Carrick and Fernandes met at United's Carrington training ground for talks that were separate to a wider meeting of the full squad to discuss a way forward from their current predicament, the Press Association reported.

Fernandes appeared to question Carrick's tactics in the wake of last week's 4-1 Champions League loss to Como, and was dropped for Sunday's Premier League match at home to Bournemouth, remaining on the bench throughout as United fell to stunning 3-0 loss that piled the pressure on Carrick.

However, after the talks, Fernandes is now considered available for the crunch match away to Chelsea on Saturday, according to reports.

Sunday's result left United down in 16th place in the Premier League with only one league win -- over newly-promoted Ipswich -- this term.

Many observers had expected the axe to fall on the boss in the wake of Sunday's defeat, but Carrick took training on Tuesday with the club resolving to give the 45-year-old more time to turn things around.

Fernandes was the second player to make outspoken comments in a post-match interview in the space of two weeks, with Lisandro Martínez having taken aim at the club's hierarchy in an explosive interview following the 2-0 Champions League loss to Atlético Madrid on Oct.13.

Carrick took charge of the team in January, stabilising the club after Ruben Amorim's often turbulent reign, overseeing an excellent run of results which culminated in a third-placed finish and a return to the Champions League.

The popular former United midfielder was rewarded with a two-year deal in the summer, but just five months after signing it he has come under major scrutiny with United having won only two of their 12 matches in all competitions, those against Ipswich and Champions League minnows Sabah.

- Michael Carrick to lead Man United vs. Chelsea amid uncertain future - sources

- Gary Neville: 'Really surprised' but 'happy' Michael Carrick set to continue as Man United boss

- Wayne Rooney's son, Kai scores, 4 goals for Man United under-18s vs. Burnley

But while Carrick's position in the dugout means he faces much of the scrutiny, Martínez's comments in Madrid focused higher up the chain of command.

Director of Football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada are also under the microscope after what is seen as a failure to properly strengthen the squad in the summer, when United put all their focus on midfield reinforcements but failed to sign either a left-back or a striker.

On Sunday at Old Trafford, it was notable that fans continued to sing Carrick's name while also turning their fire on those higher up.

Carrick received applause as he acknowledged the crowd after the match but as soon as he went into the tunnel, loud boos rained down on the players remaining on the pitch.

There was good news for Carrick and United on the injury front on Wednesday as Kobbie Mainoo returned to training.

Mainoo suffered an injury in the 1-1 draw with Tottenham on Oct. 10 and has missed United's last four matches.

Information from PA contributed to this report.

stories.headline: Who is this year's Mr. October? Tracking the playoff MVP for 2026
stories.summary: We go inside the numbers on the players doing the most to help their teams win.
stories.body:
Who is hero of the 2026 MLB playoffs?

To try to answer to that question, we're tabulating the cumulative win probability added figures for every player in the postseason. But we've added a twist: The deeper we get into the playoffs, the more weight the WPA carries. The division series counts double the wild-card round, then we'll double it again for the championship series and, finally, once again for the World Series.

This means that players who shine in the early rounds can still get on the leaderboard, but it's more difficult. Coming through when the championship leverage is at its highest is what becoming an October hero is all about.

Tuesday's hero: If not for the cracks that finally appeared in the Brewers' bullpen in Game 4, Cooper Pratt would have cemented his name in the pantheon of Wisconsin sports heroes with his go-ahead homer in the top of the 12th. It was his fourth hit of the game and two of the first three produced WPA figures that were among the top 10 plays of the night. The wild swings late in the game produced all sorts of double-digit HeroAXE changes and if not for Pratt, all of the Rays involved in the winning rally would have been close to taking this slot. Not for nothing: Another scoreless outing for Aaron Ashby adds to a playoff WPA total that has lapped the field.

Methodology
As mentioned above, each player's win probability added (WPA) is tracked on a per-game basis. Each round of the playoffs counts double that of the previous round. The tabulation is then converted to an AXE-style index in which 100 represents the average for all postseason players. The "Change" column looks in the changes in AXE numbers from the previous day for players who were in action. You can sort this column by clicking on it to see the day's heroes.

stories.headline: Sergio Pérez signs new deal with Cadillac until 2029
stories.summary: Sergio Pérez has signed a new deal with Cadillac which will see him stay with the American team until 2029.
stories.body:
Sergio Pérez has signed a new deal with Cadillac which will see him stay with the American team until 2029.

The Mexican joined the newcomers ahead of this season after taking a year's sabbatical following his exit from Red Bull at the end of the 2024 campaign, and has now committed to three more seasons with Cadillac.

The announcement coincides with the 36-year-old's 300th race in Formula 1, the Mexico City Grand Prix in his home nation.

"Joining Cadillac Formula 1 Team from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter," Pérez said in a statement.

"Building a Formula 1 team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding. There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed for the next three years."

Ahead of the weekend, Pérez is set to take to the streets of Mexico City for a show run at Paseo de la Reforma.

A six-time Grand Prix winner, Pérez is one of three drivers who are without a point so far this season, alongside teammate Valtteri Bottas and Aston Martin's Lance Stroll.

"I want to thank Dan [Towriss], Mark [Reuss], and everyone at TWG Motorsports and General Motors for the opportunity to build on what we have started together," Pérez added.

"To every member of this special team, at the track, in the U.S., the U.K., and our fans, thank you for your support and trust. I won't let you down. Let's keep pushing!"

stories.headline: It's still the age of Volkanovski in MMA pound-for-pound rankings
stories.summary: At age 38, UFC featherweight champion makes big jump in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
Alexander Volkanovski made a bold statement at UFC 333 that, even at age 38, he isn't ready to surrender his place among the greatest in MMA. The ESPN pound-for-pound voting panel took note.

On the strength of Volkanovski's second-round knockout of previously undefeated Movsar Evloev on Saturday, the UFC featherweight champion makes a big jump in the latest men's rankings. Volkanovski is No. 2, after entering the weekend five positions lower.

Volkanovski was so impressive that he outshined the co-main event performance of Petr Yan, who defended the men's bantamweight title by beating former champion Merab Dvalishvili. Yan drops one spot to No. 3, the position Dvalishvili used to occupy. Dvalishvili is now tied for eighth after his second straight loss to Yan in their fiery trilogy.

The other significant change near the top of the rankings is the disappearance of Tom Aspinall. The former UFC heavyweight champion is still healing from eye injuries suffered in a no-contest against Ciryl Gane in October 2025. Because Aspinall has not fought in over a year, he is ineligible for the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Oct. 28. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Previous ranking: 7

Record: 29-4

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Movsar Evloev, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (38) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. He did just that by handing Evloev his first loss at UFC 333.

3. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Previous ranking: 2

Record: 21-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career, then completing his trilogy with Dvalishvili with a successful title defense. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet.

4. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

5. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: Tied for 4

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: Jan. 30 vs. Manel Kape

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch at UFC 331. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

7. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from a challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

T-8. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Previous ranking: 3

Record: 21-6

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Oct. 24

Next: TBA

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. Their third meeting at UFC 333 was the most competitive in their trilogy, but Dvalishvili fell short again.

T-8. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight on the White House lawn. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Alex Pereira

UFC heavyweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 13-4

Last: L (TKO2) vs. Ciryl Gane, June 14

Next: Dec. 12 vs. Sergei Pavlovich

Pereira made a big splash in the MMA after a world championship career in kickboxing. He joined the UFC in 2021 and became a middleweight champion the following year, then moved on to be a two-time light heavyweight titlist before making an unprecedented bid for a belt in a third weight class when he fought Game at UFC Freedom 250 for an interim heavyweight title. Pereira got knocked out in that fight, but now he's back on his feet and in position to reclaim his position when he faces a fellow title contender, Pavlovich, at UFC 335.

Other fighters receiving votes: Alexandre Pantoja and Sean Strickland.

How our panel voted
Brett Okamoto: 1. Islam Makhachev; 2. Petr Yan; 3. Ilia Topuria; 4. Alexander Volkanovski; 5. Joshua Van; 6. Arman Tsarukyan; 7. Merab Dvalishvili; 8. Ciryl Gane; 9. Alex Pereira; 10. Justin Gaethje.

Carlos Contreras Legaspi: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Gaethje; 4. Topuria; 5. Yan; 6. Van; 7. Pereira; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Tsarukyan.

Andrew Davis: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Gane; 8. Tsarukyan; 9 Pereira; 10. Sean Strickland.

Dre Waters: 1. Makhachev; 2. Volkanovski; 3. Yan; 4. Gaethje; 5. Topuria; 6. Van; 7. Dvalishvili; 8. Gane; 9. Pereira; 10. Tsarukyan.

Jeff Wagenheim: 1. Makhachev; 2. Yan; 3. Volkanovski; 4. Van; 5. Gaethje; 6. Tsarukyan; 7. Topuria; 8. Dvalishvili; 9. Gane; 10. Alexandre Pantoja.

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which Natalia Silva captured by beating Wang Cong at UFC 332. When Shevchenko is healed up, she'll be looking to take back the belt.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight champion

Record: 21-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Wang Cong, Oct. 3

Next: TBA

Silva was looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Rose Namajunas at UFC 324. And now she has fulfilled that expectation, beating Wang at UFC 332 to win the belt vacated by injured Valentina Shevchenko. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027.

5. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Virna Jandiroba

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

10. Virna Jandiroba

UFC strawweight

Record: 23-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Tabatha Ricci, April 4

Next: Nov. 7 vs. Tatiana Suarez

Jandiroba fell short in last October's fight with Mackenzie Dern for the vacant title, but she bounced back in April with a victory over Ricci. Up next is a top-10 showdown with Suarez, who also lost a title challenge last year. The winner will be right back in the championship mix.

Other fighter receiving votes: Joselyne Edwards and Jasmine Jasudavicius.

stories.headline: The NHL's one-month breakout, rebound players: Who keeps it up?
stories.summary: Each team has played at least 10 games, giving us a sample of players with an elevated level of play.
stories.body:
The 2026-27 NHL season is well underway, with each team having played at least 10 games through the first month.

Based on this early-season sample, more than a few players have taken a huge leap forward in their play, or they've rebounded after recent down seasons. Naturally, the improvement from the players has elevated the performance of their teams and made for an exciting beginning to the campaign. There are two parts to this list below: players who have raised their ceiling with their elevated play, and players who have rebounded after down years.

It isn't solely about production -- it is about controlling play, impacting the game in a more meaningful way, playing higher in the lineup and thriving. Production is a major part of the evaluative process, but becoming a more impactful player for the team is likely to be more sustainable over the balance of the season, rather than benefiting from an elevated shooting percentage.

The rebounds

Auston Matthews

C, Toronto Maple Leafs
The Leafs made a lot of moves this offseason and look much better for it, but none of it matters unless their captain returned to form.

After two seasons that saw his production and ability to control the game fall dramatically, Matthews looks back to his dominant self.

Matthews has scored nine goals through 14 games and is on pace to notch 54 total and score 120 points this season. He's dominating offensively, finishing at a rate more typical of his talent, and is driving the Leafs up the standings with his play.

Matthews' skating has looked noticeably better. According to NHL Edge, Matthews has jumped from the 52nd and 72nd percentiles in 20-22 mph and 18-20 mph bursts in 2025-26, to the 68th and 93rd percentiles this season. He has been far more involved off the puck, specifically on the forecheck, resulting in his line forcing turnovers, extending offensive zone time and creating more scoring chances.

The combination of his improved health, a top-five power play and an elevated shooting percentage have led to good play on and off the puck, leading to a noticeable rebound in impact and production.

Elias Pettersson

C, Vancouver Canucks
Pettersson may be the only player with more coverage than Matthews. There has been no shortage of negative off-ice noise plaguing the Canucks center over the past few seasons, and that doesn't account for how poor the on-ice play has been either.

The Canucks are going through a rebuild, and tried to trade Pettersson on numerous occasions over the past two seasons. Under a new coaching staff, he has looked less like a player skating with the weight of the world on his shoulders and more like a top-six difference-maker. On a point-per-game pace, Pettersson has shown signs that the Petey of old is coming back to life, specifically the one-timers on the PP.

Pettersson is drawing penalties at an elite rate, has already equaled his power-play goal total from last season, and is driving play through zone entries, shot assists and excellent defensive play. He's producing points at even strength that is in line for a top-six-caliber forward, and a fringe top-line player. Pettersson ranks top five in blocked shots among NHL forwards, and is much more engaged that the previous two seasons.

In the long term, if 2026 first-round pick Caleb Malhotra can be a top-line center for Vancouver, it will allow Pettersson to play a second-line role, while producing at a high level on the power play. In the short term, Pettersson's resurgence gives the Canucks a legitimate top-six option in the rebuild if he can keep his play consistent.

Linus Ullmark

G, Ottawa Senators
Prior to Ullmark getting hurt, he was one of the best goalies to start the season and earned his spot on this list. At 8.4 goals above expected, per Moneypuck, he ranks second in the NHL behind Jake Oettinger.

Without Jake Sanderson for the first part of the season, Ullmark backstopped the Sens, covering for a defensive group missing its best defender. Furthermore, the Sens have taken a slight step back defensively as a team, and Ullmark has been the key piece to a few important points. He has already surpassed last year's wins above replacement value. Prior to injury, Ullmark looked more balanced in goal, sharp in his movements and challenging shooters without being overly aggressive.

Ullmark's time in Ottawa has been challenging at times, working through poor play and publicly addressing mental health struggles, among other things. To come back in Jennings Trophy form out of the gate and be lost to injury is a cruel twist of fate. The expectation is that Ullmark will return in the next week, however goaltending injuries are unpredictable.

The drop-off from Ullmark to Samuel Ersson (and others) is chasmic, given the way Ullmark started the season. The Sens are hoping he's in early-season form when he returns.

The breakouts

Alexis Lafreniere

LW, New York Rangers
It is odd that a player who is entering his seventh NHL season would find himself on this list, but the 2020 first overall pick has had a rough go in the early part of his NHL career. He has played for coaches more interested in winning than developing a potential young star and giving him opportunities with talented veterans.

In fact, the Rangers have a long track record of struggling to develop young draft picks, and many have succeeded elsewhere after struggling in the Rangers system as young players (K'Andre Miller, Kaapo Kakko, Pavel Buchnevich, Brett Howden). Lafreniere is finally getting top-line minutes, averaging 19 minutes per game, and is showing much of the play-driving ability that made him worthy of the first overall pick.

One of the more noticeable things about Lafreniere is the difference in his play since the departure of Artemi Panarin. Lafreniere deferred to Panarin more than he should have in his development years. Without Panarin -- and no longer serving as the young player on his line, that would be Gabe Perreault -- Lafreniere is creating scoring chances through his own assertive play. He's adjusted to his new role, and started to execute some of the reads he makes on and off the puck, which has buoyed his confidence.

His zone entries have improved dramatically, leading to more scoring chances off the rush and a greater ability to create for his line mates. His improved patience on and off the puck have led to better play execution and results. His shooting percentage will regress at some point, but his impact defensively and ability to anticipate the play should continue to allow Lafreniere to be a difference-maker for the Rangers.

Easton Cowan

RW, Toronto Maple Leafs
Giddy up, indeed! Cowan looks like a completely different hockey player this season under new coach Jim Hiller. After starting on the third line, Cowan's play forced the coach's hand, and he has looked like a true difference-maker on the top line with Auston Matthews and Jack Roslovic.

Once thought of as a middle-six complementary player, Cowan has raised his ceiling to a potential difference-maker on the top line. Cowan is half way to equaling his production of 11 goals and 29 points in his rookie year, with six goals and 13 points through 14 games. His points-per-game pace has doubled, partially because of increased opportunity -- but it is a well-earned opportunity.

Cowan is playing on both special teams, he's a dogged forechecker, and is part of a line that is controlling play in their matchups. Cowan has gained a step in his skating; it's showing up in the NHL Edge data -- he's in the 90-plus percentiles in all three burst categories. That's allowed him to become a more dangerous rush attacker, beat defenders, win races to loose pucks and force turnovers all over the ice.

He stops on pucks, drives the net and is using his skating to attack the dangerous areas of the ice. He's more confident making skilled plays and is now working with players capable of capitalizing on the chances he creates. If this is who Cowan is, it is a major development for a team that desperately needs to find in-house solutions with a significant lack of resources available to execute significant trades.

Matvei Michkov

RW, Philadelphia Flyers
Finally! The Flyers had about the worst start possible, but Michkov is showing signs of the elite talent many were expecting after he was drafted seventh overall in 2023.

He's not playing in the best development environment from a coaching perspective, but he's making the best of it. After an excellent summer that saw Michkov show up to camp in the best shape of his career, he leads the Flyers in points. His shooting percentage is absolutely not going to sustain itself, but he's matched his power-play goal output from last season already.

With eight goals through 14 games, it is reasonable to believe Michkov will notch his first 30-goal season as his shooting percentage normalizes. Even netting 35 is a distinct possibility, especially if he continues to score on the power play.

Not only is Michkov scoring at an impressive clip, he looks more confident in the plays he makes on a regular basis. He's unafraid to hold the puck and wait out opponents to take advantage, with the perfect example coming against the Colorado Avalanche. He has used his tremendous puck skill and elite hockey sense to create chances every night, and has been one of the best Flyers to start the season.

One would hope that as he continues to play well, he is rewarded with more ice time, and does not get stuck behind guys who are not capable of producing at his level.

Mason McTavish

C, St. Louis Blues
A change of scenery has yielded incredible results for McTavish. After falling completely out of the picture in Anaheim, McTavish is playing a regular top-six role in St. Louis and is on pace to smash his career highs in goals (22) and points (52).

For the first time in his career, he's above 50% expected goals, and creating more chances than he's surrendering while on the ice. His shooting percentage is elevated, but not completely unsustainable over a single season. McTavish has fit like a glove in the Blues' lineup and the system is allowing him to create more.

McTavish's microstats haven't seen a tremendous jump, but the elevated opportunity to work with skilled players has allowed him to thrive. McTavish is getting to the middle of the ice on a more consistent basis and is in the 97th percentile for high-danger shots, according to NHL Edge.

The biggest concern with McTavish has been his foot speed. While he's unlikely to ever be a premier skater, he has looked noticeably quicker to start the season. He has shown a greater understanding of his physical makeup -- and how to utilize it in the middle of the ice. McTavish's step forward and the increased opportunity has made him one of the best Blues to start the season and key part of their offense.

Vasily Podkolzin

RW, Edmonton Oilers
The moment the young Russian winger was the third man on the "McDrai" line, he was highly likely to break out.

Podkolzin wasn't drafted to be the player who puts up 40 goals and 95 points. He was thought of as a power forward who was going to be extraordinarily difficult to play against, while possessing the talent to capitalize playing with elite talent. Well, there is no greater elite talent than Connor McDavid or Leon Draisaitl. Podkolzin's ability and willingness to do the dirty work, be it retrieving pucks, winning puck battles or playing elite defense has made him a staple on that line.

Podkolzin is on pace for more than 50 goals and 90 points, and while the goal total is a stretch, he's a younger version of Zach Hyman who scored 54 goals with eerily similar deployment in the Oilers lineup. His net-front presence makes him a premier target because it is one that disrupts goalies and defenders, and allows him to be available for rebounds and deflections.

Defensively, he's proved to be one Edmonton's best forwards, earning the trust of the coaching staff to play in critical situations. Podkolzin is at a completely different level than his first few seasons, is playing nearly 20 minutes per game, and is exactly the type of cheap-contract forward the Oilers need to get tremendous value out of if they are to contend for Stanley Cup.

stories.headline: Valkyries look to clinch, Dream try to stay alive in Game 6 of the WNBA Finals
stories.summary: How did Golden State take control? Can Atlanta gets its offense going? And will the 12:30 tip impact the outcome?
stories.byline: Kareem Copeland and Alexa Philippou and Michael Voepel
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- Seven-game playoff series are known for having major momentum swings. That has been the case for the 2026 WNBA Finals, only the second year the championship series has had a best-of-seven format.

The Atlanta Dream looked firmly in control following back-to-back wins in Games 2 and 3 to pull ahead 2-1. But the Golden State Valkyries have snagged the momentum back with consecutive wins in Games 4 and 5 to take a 3-2 lead.

With a victory in Game 6 on Thursday (12:30 p.m. ET) at Atlanta's State Farm Arena, the Valkyries would win the WNBA title in just their second season, while a victory for the Dream would send the series back to Ballhalla for a winner-take-all Game 7 on Halloween in San Francisco.

ESPN looks at how the series changed and what both teams need to do to come out on top Thursday.

How did the Valkyries go from down 2-1 to one win away from the WNBA title?

Copeland: Turnovers have been the biggest predictor of success in these Finals. In its Game 2 and 3 losses, Golden State averaged 18 turnovers that led to 23 points for Atlanta. In the Game 4 and 5 wins, the Valkyries averaged nine turnovers that turned into seven points. On the flip side, in Games 4 and 5, the Dream averaged 17.5 turnovers that led to 18.5 points for the Valkyries. If there's a silo of metrics that I've paid the most attention to, it's turnovers, turnover differential and points scored off those turnovers.

Philippou: Credit Natalie Nakase for the adjustments she made after Game 3. The Valkyries are the first team in WNBA Finals history to change multiple players in their starting lineup in Game 3 or later of a best-of-five series (without an injury to a starter). But it has paid dividends for Golden State to start Kaila Charles and Tiffany Hayes while bringing Kayla Thornton and Cecilia Zandalasini off the bench.

Nakase has also shortened her rotation to basically seven players instead of the usual nine or 10, with Kiah Stokes, Veronica Burton and Gabby Williams each playing closer to 30 minutes per game this series. Altogether, the moves have helped the Valkyries have better starts and get back to their defensive identity. The coach has credited her "egoless" team for being willing to make individual sacrifices to win, and now it is one victory away from a championship.

What must the Valkyries keep doing to win the championship?

Copeland: Keep making life hard for Angel Reese. The three-time All-Star and 2026 Defensive Player of the Year was the runaway favorite for Finals MVP when the Dream led 2-1. In Game 4, she was held to 2-for-12 shooting, eight points, nine rebounds and six turnovers. Things weren't much better in Game 5 as Reese was limited to seven points, 15 rebounds and five assists on 2-for-8 shooting. She seemed outwardly frustrated Monday night after averaging 25.5 points and 14 rebounds in the two Atlanta victories. (Oh, and winning the turnover differential.)

Voepel: There haven't been a lot of what you would call easy baskets in this series, but in the past two games the Valkyries have gotten more of them than the Dream. Mostly, that has been through steals leading to layups, but they also have been successful at finding a few gaps in Atlanta's defense. A few times, they've just worn out the Dream with their patience until the end of the shot clock, when they've finally gotten a good look.

Nakase talked a lot Monday about how she has a tendency to be a little impatient and want things too quickly and had to slow down for her team. The Valkyries have not let the Dream dictate pace the past two games. Instead, Golden State has been in control, and if the Valkyries can do it again Thursday, it will be hard for Atlanta to have a much different result than in Games 4 and 5.

In addition to Golden State's defense, what has gone wrong for the Dream?

Philippou: For as spectacular as Reese was in Games 2 and 3, Atlanta's margin for error is just so much narrower if it is this reliant on her to win. Rhyne Howard, Allisha Gray and Jordin Canada are averaging 14.4, 12.0 and 10.6 points, respectively, in the series. Scoring was always going to be difficult to come by in a matchup of two defensive juggernauts, but the Dream are undoubtedly better offensively than they showed Monday -- not to mention they are more offensively minded than the Valkyries. Atlanta's guards need to get going for the Dream to have any hope of winning the championship.

I'm also wondering how much fatigue is a factor for the Dream, not that they're likely to admit it, given how much they've relied on their top six players this series and all year. We'll see how both clubs look in Game 6 following another cross-country trip, with two days of rest in between games.

Voepel: The Dream are a tight-knit unit, but the past two games they haven't played together as well as the Valkyries have. There are moments when players' individual frustrations have seemed to bubble over more on the Dream's side because they just haven't been able to run their offense the way they did against other teams. Before the Finals, both clubs downplayed the regular-season series, won 3-0 by Golden State, because all those games were so much earlier this year. But it's looking more like those results were an indicator of why the Valkyries might have an upper hand in this series.

And while no one for Atlanta has used this as an excuse, Gray's hand injury has impacted her effectiveness. She averaged 19.0 points and shot 46.2% from the field in the regular season, compared to 13.9 points and 34.4% in her eight playoff games. That's a significant factor in Atlanta's effectiveness and her confidence, especially against a defensive team this good.

What must Atlanta do to stay alive and force Game 7?

Copeland: Find a way to score. Yes, Atlanta was one of the best defensive teams in the league during the regular season, but it also ranked No. 3 in points per game (91.3). That was a huge part of the Dream's identity that has been essentially eradicated in all but one Finals contest. Gray (19.0 points per game) was the No. 9 scorer in the league, Howard (17.7) was No. 11 and Reese (16.4) was No. 17. The Valkyries were the No. 14 scoring team in the WNBA, so they're absolutely used to winning low-scoring slugfests. That's exactly how they got to this point. The Dream relied on their offense much more, and when that is taken away, life became much more difficult.

As Mike said above, Gray is not 100%, so that's a blow. But when a team is averaging 31 fewer points in three Finals losses than it's used to during the regular season, that's a considerable shift in the ethos of how it operates as a group. A boost from DeWanna Bonner, who has been held to single digits in all five Finals games, would be a help.

Philippou: Can Reese and the Dream rediscover the confidence and fire they exuded earlier in this series? Atlanta is a team that tends to be more emotive than Golden State -- the highs are high; the lows can be low. Neither group is that experienced on this stage, but the Dream's young stars -- Reese, Howard and Gray -- are entirely new to the roller coaster that a seven-game championship series can entail.

The Valkyries pride themselves on being at their best when their backs are against the wall. The Dream need to take a similar approach and keep the belief high that they can still win this series despite tough setbacks in the past two games.

Will the 12:30 p.m. ET tipoff impact Game 6?

Copeland: Not on the court. I look at this in the same way as some questions about motivation at this point of the series and season. If someone can't get themselves fired up at this point with the biggest opportunity of their professional career, at maximum, 80 minutes away, then there's something wrong. Both teams are dealing with the same issues regarding the cadence of the series -- back and forth across Pacific and Eastern time zones. But if an early afternoon start throws off either team in any drastic measure, particularly from an energy standpoint, that's an internal issue. Sure, it might be an odd time, but it's not like these two clubs have been shooting the lights out and the early start would mess with their rhythm.

stories.headline: Power to burn and a 'trademark' goal: why Ethan Drever has rocketed up draft boards
stories.summary: Growing up an Essendon supporter, Ethan Drever hasn't 'seen anything' like success. But his rise up draft boards could have him in the frame to be his childhood club's first pick, writes Jasper Chellappah.
stories.body:
Ethan Drever had absolutely no choice on his AFL team. As a newborn he was put in an Essendon jumper at the hospital and he's been a Bomber ever since.

It's been a rough 18 years of fandom since, and he's got some thoughts about his dad's decision.

"I'm [born in] 2008, I haven't seen anything!" he tells ESPN with a grin - and a grimace.

"Dad tells me about his success and I'm like, 'You don't have to rub it in like that.'"

The Dons are entering a new era in 2027 under Mark McVeigh and it's being driven through the draft. They snagged Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow, and Dyson Sharp in the first round 12 months ago and now own pick 1 in the upcoming draft.

Drever also has a lot of thoughts about those drafted before him.

"They've got some good young boys in there now. Robey, Sharp, they're gonna be so good.

"I like Farrow. He should be kicking in and doing all that, he needs to be in priority positions. That's what he's gonna be doing in the future.

"Just that halfback, I reckon he's gonna be really good... he's a beautiful left foot kick."

After a dour two-win season the Bombers have first call on Drever, with the 188cm on-baller strongly linked at the top of the board.

He's an electric runner with the intent to tackle, chase, and pressure - something that hasn't been a trait of Essendon's list for a long time.

Asked what he thinks when watching his boyhood club each weekend, Drever's response would prick the ears of all Bombers fans.

"It'd be nice to be out there and sort of help the boys out, that's kinda what I'm thinking!"

The Vic Country MVP and Rebels best and fairest produced a remarkable season. His star has risen from a first-round chance to the very top of the open pool.

He may have the most translatable traits to AFL level of any prospect. Drever is an elite power athlete, recording a 2.92 second 20 metre sprint which comes across in the tape. He bursts out of the contest with driving legs and loves to exit forward of the stoppage to inflict maximum damage.

His ultra consistent season has come about without any injury concerns, something all other top prospects this year haven't been able to say.

"It's been good not to have to sit on the sidelines this year at all and I can just keep playing consistent footy," he says.

"I only missed one [game] which was just after champs, I just had a break."

Drever lays claim to a pretty handy trademark. On six separate occasions this season he's collected the ball -- either out of a stoppage or in open play -- and powered away from opponents into the forward half of the ground.

From there his long running gait and elite top speed helps him separate from chasing defenders and break the paint of 50 to drive home sensational goals.

"I have heard it's called the trademark goal now. I don't know where that's really come from, it's just a natural thing I guess. I just like to run and have a ping from outside 50," Drever tells ESPN.

"Definitely one of my traits is just my power, especially this year. Building up over the pre-season and definitely my two-way running.

"It's the long-term goal to move into the midfield and be a bit of a Jordan Dawson with his two-way running. I love Finn Callaghan, how he plays. Those two are really great role models for me.

"I think Hugh McCluggage as well, I've watched him a lot. I had a meeting with him this year, he's that sort of two-way runner as well and he's been really good for me."

Drever played 13 games for the Rebels this year in amongst commitments with the AFL Academy and Vic Country. He collected the ball 28 times to go with a goal a game, but he's not satisfied with just being an offensive weapon.

The Ballarat local is a tenacious presence in contests with the appetite to chase and tackle, racking up 6.5 per outing to frank his status as the best pure midfielder in the open pool.

At the draft combine he showed off a much-improved engine running a 6:27 minute 2km after going 20 seconds slower in the lead-up. It's a time that will put him towards the front of the pack on day one of pre-season.

Drever knows exactly what's required to be a midfielder at the next level, and he's determined to get there as soon as possible.

"My endurance side was a big goal of mine, obviously at the top level you've just got to be able to run all day.

"Honing in on my fundamentals and trying to get them the best I can as well. That's what the most important thing is because it's the little one percenters that make a difference in the AFL.

Drever is now on the precipice of living out his dream of becoming an AFL player, and it could be for his boyhood club as the top choice in the open pool of the draft.

That won't matter to him, so long as he gets his opportunity to shine on the big stage.

"I don't really care [if I go at pick 1]. It's nice to have my name up in consideration alongside those boys but I'll just be happy to be picked up wherever I go."

stories.headline: Lens fans banned from Liverpool match for throwing flares vs. Brugge
stories.summary: Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling Tuesday.
stories.body:
NYON, Switzerland -- Fans of Ligue 1 club Lens were banned from buying tickets for a Champions League game at Liverpool by a UEFA disciplinary ruling on Tuesday.

Lens fans lit dozens of flares and threw some toward rival supporters and the field, forcing the team's Champions League game at Club Brugge last week to be stopped briefly. Lens lost 3-0.

The club already were on probation by UEFA for fans lighting flares and fireworks at a previous Champions League game at Slavia Prague in September.

UEFA said its appeals judges imposed a ban on Lens selling tickets to fans for two Champions League away games.

The sanction will be served when Lens play at Leipzig on Nov. 24 and at Liverpool at Anfield on Jan. 27. A third game ban is deferred for a two-year probationary period.

UEFA said Lens were fined €80,000 ($89,000) for charges of "lighting and throwing of pyrotechnics as well as for acts of damage."

stories.headline: Bafana boss Pitso Mosimane's latest South Africa squad shows favouritism fears were unfounded
stories.summary: Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.
stories.body:
When Pitso Mosimane returned as Bafana Bafana head coach, sceptics feared that his proximity to South African club football would lead to an erosion of the meritocratic culture Hugo Broos had built, but the 62-year-old's second preliminary squad suggests it has only been enhanced.

Mosimane began his tenure with Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying wins over Guinea and Eritrea and a friendly victory over Egypt. Next up is the AFCON qualifying double-header against Kenya on Nov. 13 & 17.

Mosimane has made several changes from his first preliminary squad, which he announced almost immediately after taking charge at the beginning of September.

Chicago Fire's Mbekezeli Mbokazi has returned from injury, while Aden McCarthy, Botiumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Luke le Roux, Thalente Mbatha, Nkosikhona Radebe, Devin Titus and Thakasani Mbanjwa have also received call-ups.

For every one of these call-ups, a layman can deduce a clear possible motive. McCarthy is the most obvious among them -- he has consistently featured at centre-back for Sabah in the UEFA Champions League and performed well at the highest level.

Radiopane and Xulu are in hot scoring form domestically for Orlando Pirates and Richards Bay respectively. Titus has earned his place with a strong start to life at MAS Fes in Morocco. Mbatha is back from injury and le Roux on the books of a new club at Cercle Brugge after struggling for game time at Portsmouth.

Radebe adds a right-back option from an in-form AmaZulu side with Mamelodi Sundowns' Khuliso Mudau still on the mend from injury. Mbanjwa is rewarded for a strong start to the season in goal for Golden Arrows.

Yanela Mbuthuma and Shandre Campbell -- both of whom have experienced dips in form and fortune at club level since the last international break -- are notable absentees.

In cutting two players he had given opportunities to after they had been mostly overlooked by Broos, Mosimane suggested he is willing to operate without fear or favour.

When 'Jingles' was on the verge of being appointed, Broos was quoted as telling Het Nieuwsblad: "You know, South Africa still don't have a coach. The candidate is Pitso Mosimane, a successful South African coach.

"But they know that if he comes in, they'll go five years back in time. Club owners and agents calling coaches to influence the squad selection. I threw all of them out. If one called, I would say bluntly: 'I don't talk with agents'."

The concern over agents and owners trying their luck in influencing the Bafana head coach may have been well-founded. Broos was not the first to complain of this within the national team setup.

However, questioning if Mosimane himself was open to influence without proof he was willing to make publicly available was ill-advised. It is impossible to accurately speculate on what conversations have or have not gone on between Mosimane and club owners and agents in the two months since then, but what is clear is that his team selection has been thoroughly meritocratic.

The momentum he has garnered is reminiscent of what Broos achieved in the first six months of his tenure.

At the time, the Belgian's irreverent team selection and approach to squad culture put everybody on their toes and led to an uptick in results. After they had failed to qualify for AFCON 2021 immediately before Broos was appointed, the Belgian fell narrowly short of steering Bafana into qualification playoffs for the 2022 World Cup.

In subsequent years, he kicked on and led Bafana to third place at AFCON 2023 (held belatedly in Ivory Coast in early 2024) and the 2026 World Cup round of 32.

When discussing the most successful Bafana Bafana coaches of all-time, Broos should be placed alongside Clive Barker in the top two. However, even the brightest tacticians eventually settle on patterns in their squad selection, and towards the end of his tenure, the Belgian became more predictable in certain aspects.

There was a fairly settled back five of Ronwen Williams, Aubrey Modiba, Mbokazi, Ime Okon and Mudau, and until he switched up his attacking plan to revive the FIFA World Cup campaign, Broos was likely to start Lyle Foster upfront with Evidence Makgopa the main alternative.

In midfield, Teboho Mokoena was a near certain starter and Sphephelo Sithole the clear preferred option alongside him, although Broos occasionally tinkered with his formation and left room for the likes of Bathusi Aubaas and the late Jayden Adams in the holding role. Nkosinathi Sibisi was considered another option, occasionally stepping out from the back into midfield.

Mosimane's arrival has reopened competition for places in these positions. Brooklyn Poggenpoel is retained in the squad after impressing in midfield over the last international break.

After Mbuthuma's minutes upfront, Radiopane and Xulu have been given a chance to earn theirs. Foster has made a second successive preliminary squad, although he failed to make the final squad last time out while in the process of leaving Burnley on loan to Houston Dynamo and settling in.

Fawaaz Basadien, Olwethu Makhanya, and McCarthy are in consideration in the backline. Mudau is, however, still the likely first-choice at right-back for the time being when he returns to full fitness. Still, Mosimane has done well to identify alternatives.

Mosimane declined to get drawn into a war of words with Broos over anything not directly related to matters on the pitch and instead praised his predecessor's impressive record as Bafana head coach.

In his first stint, Mosimane may not have succeeded in the hotseat. However, early results and his approach to team selection suggest he has justified the decision of the South African Football Association (SAFA) to give him a second chance and trust him to navigate the role without fear or favour to anyone.

Bafana Preliminary squad for Kenya (Nov. 13 & 17)
GK: Ronwen Williams, Sipho Chaine, Ricardo Gass, Thakasani Mbanjwa

DEF: Aubrey Modiba, Samukele Kabini, Fawaaz Basadien, Nkosikhona Radebe, Thapelo Morena, Thabang Matuludi, Olwethu Makhanya, Khulumani Ndamane, Ime Okon, Lebone Seema, Nkosinathi Sibisi, Mbekezeli Mbokazi, Aden McCarthy

MID: Teboho Mokoena, Lebohang Maboe, Sphephelo Sithole, Bathusi Aubaas, Brooklyn Poggenpoel, Thalente Mbatha, Luke le Roux

FWD: Iqraam Rayners, Cassius Mailula, Oswin Appollis, Tashreeq Matthews, Relebohile Mofokeng, Themba Zwane, Thapelo Maseko, Luther Singh, Devin Titus, Lyle Foster, Boitumelo Radiopane, Nqaba Xulu, Tshepang Moremi, Puso Dithejane

stories.headline: NRL transfer whispers: Flegler move likely; Cowboys keen to keep Nanai
stories.summary: The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1. Isaac Issa has news from the Dragons on some key outside backs
stories.body:
The NRL season may be over, but the player market is already heating up ahead of November 1, with clubs beginning to shape their rosters for 2027 and beyond.

From player movement to changes behind the scenes, ESPN NRL Insider Isaac Issa has the latest whispers from around the competition.

Flegler move looking likely
Tom Flegler is looking likely to leave the Dolphins at the end of 2027, with ESPN understanding the prop is leaning towards a move away from the club.

While Flegler is yet to make a firm decision, the Dolphins are now facing the prospect of losing him for the 2028 season and beyond.

His future shapes as a situation to watch as the November 1 contracting window approaches.

Cowboys keen to keep Nanai
North Queensland remain keen to retain Jeremiah Nanai, with ESPN understanding the Cowboys are hopeful the back-rower will extend his stay despite preparing to test his value on the open market from November 1.

Nanai has been with the club since he was a teenager, developing into a Queensland Origin representative, and the Cowboys are hopeful that connection will help keep him in Townsville.

Samrani expected to test open market
Jordan Samrani is expected to test the open market from November 1. ESPN understands he will explore his options for 2028 and beyond.

Following a breakout season with the Parramatta Eels, Samrani is open to assessing opportunities elsewhere when the contracting window opens on Sunday.

Cochrane set to link up with Titans feeder

Taye Cochrane is set to link up with Gold Coast Titans feeder club Ipswich Jets for the 2027 season following his departure from Canterbury.

ESPN understands the young fullback has signed with the Queensland Cup outfit after the Bulldogs opted against offering him a contract for next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances for Canterbury in 2026, having been part of the club's Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side in 2024.

The move follows Phil Gould's confirmation that Cochrane would leave the Bulldogs, with ESPN revealing he had not been offered a new deal.

Bulldogs opt against Cochrane deal

Canterbury have opted against offering Taye Cochrane a contract for 2027, with the young fullback set to depart Belmore.

ESPN understands Cochrane was not offered a new deal, following Phil Gould's confirmation he would not remain at the Bulldogs next season.

Cochrane scored six tries in 14 NSW Cup appearances this year, playing predominantly at fullback.

He was part of Canterbury's 2024 Jersey Flegg premiership-winning side before progressing to NSW Cup the following season.

Panthers make retention intentions clear on Patea
Penrith have informed Luron Patea's management of their desire to retain the young prop beyond 2027, although he still intends to test the open market from November 1.

ESPN understands multiple clubs are interested in speaking to Patea, who is approaching the final year of his Panthers contract.

ESPN previously reported that Penrith had yet to begin extension discussions with Patea.

Tigers keen to retain Mason

Wests Tigers are keen to retain Heath Mason, with the club working through roster space to accommodate the young utility.

ESPN understands Mason remains part of the Tigers' long-term plans, although his future is yet to be resolved ahead of 2027.

Cowboys open to keeping Taumalolo

North Queensland are open to retaining Jason Taumalolo beyond 2027, with the veteran forward's assessment of how his body is holding up set to guide the next step.

ESPN understands the Cowboys will take their lead from Taumalolo as he weighs up his playing future, reflecting his standing as a club legend.

Taumalolo is contracted until the end of next season and becomes eligible to negotiate with rival clubs for 2028 onwards from November 1.

Panthers lock in Patea
Penrith have secured Tua Patea until the end of 2029, with the youngster signing an extension that includes a pathway from a development contract into the club's top 30.

Patea capped off the 2026 season with a hat-trick in the Panthers' Jersey Flegg Grand Final victory, having started the year with an NRL training block.

The new deal will see him join Penrith's full-time NRL squad as he works towards a first-grade debut.

Bulldogs closing in on Skelton return

Jeral Skelton is closing in on a return to Canterbury following his departure from the Wests Tigers.

ESPN understands the Bulldogs are in advanced discussions to bring the outside back to the club for the 2027 season.

The former Warriors outside back joined the Dragons on a development contract this season and is set to move into the club's top 30 squad in 2027.

"I've been linked to a few a clubs," Bostock admitted.

He said that while he "obviously sees it in the media," his sole focus is the Kangaroos.

There is interest in keeping Sloan at the Dragons, but several hurdles remain before that can become a reality.

Roster space and salary cap room would need to be worked through, while any arrangement would also require Castleford to agree to release him.

Sloan previously admitted he would "love to" remain in the NRL when speaking to Channel Nine in August, after his Castleford deal had been announced.

stories.body:
The NBA is only a few games deep, but leaguewide buzz never stops.

The LeBron James and Jaylen Brown era with the Philadelphia 76ers got off to an ideal start by spoiling ring night for the New York Knicks. The Detroit Pistons also returned to their regular-season dominance with a win over the Boston Celtics, and the Oklahoma City Thunder struck the first rivalry blow against the San Antonio Spurs this season.

Now, what will Giannis Antetokounmpo's first season away from Milwaukee look like? And how will the other new faces in new places make their impact this season?

All season, bookmark this page for the latest news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders.

How Dybantsa will impact the Wizards on the court

After missing the first four games of the season with an ankle injury, No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa will make his regular-season debut on Wednesday, ESPN's Shams Charania reported.

Dybantsa's arrival could give the Wizards one of the best starting lineups in the Eastern Conference -- which would be quite a change of pace for a team that hasn't won 20 games since 2022-23. Anthony Davis has been explosive and productive through four games. Trae Young is averaging 22 points and a league-best 11 assists per game. And Kyshawn George is up to 18 PPG as he continues to make strides as an all-around NBA contributor. Add Dybantsa to that mix, and there's legitimate reason for excitement in Washington.

The only downside is that Dybantsa should command plenty of playing time, which could squeeze an already overcrowded Wizards rotation. Already, 2025 first-rounder Will Riley has seen his playing time crater, but he, Justin Champagnie, Tre Johnson and Bilal Coulibaly are all wings who will now likely come off the bench, yet deserve the opportunity to continue their development. -- Zach Kram

"We always said availability was a big factor for our team with all the guys we have out," Curry said. "It's no secret that the [center] spot is an important one for us, especially with his skill set. It's hard to talk about without keeping the humanity of it in mind. But it is a tough one to figure out."

Team sources continue to express an extreme level of pessimism that Porzingis will ever play for the Warriors again, but he could end up helping the organization in another way, because his contract, which is only guaranteed for $3 million next season, could still prove to be valuable in executing a trade.

What Edwards' injury means for Wolves

On Monday, Anthony Edwards looked like an MVP candidate as he poured in 47 points in Cleveland. On Tuesday, that dream was dashed early, as ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Edwards will miss up to two months due to right knee surgery.

Minnesota can still contend this season, as long as Edwards returns healthy at the end of that projected time frame. The partnership of Edwards and LaMelo Ball was one of the most exciting elements of the new season, and the Timberwolves raced to a 3-1 start featuring three blowout wins, with an overtime loss to the Cavaliers marring their ledger. At the end of two more months, 52 games will remain on their schedule.

But they won't be comfortable in the meantime. The Timberwolves have a relatively shallow roster, and their bench will be stretched thin once sixth man Ayo Dosunmu moves into the starting lineup to replace Edwards. Their two-way star's absence also reduces any margin for error with the rest of the roster; Ball is notoriously injury-prone, and if both guards are ever out at the same time, a lengthy losing streak could ensue.

Marks: A busy weekend of transaction expected
The last weekend of the offseason is expected to bring a flurry of transactions.

Starting on Saturday Oct. 17, teams will need to decide on players signed to non-guaranteed contracts. If a player is on the roster past 5 p.m. ET, teams will begin incurring a per day salary charge.

For example, the New York Knicks would be charged $17,622 per day against the cap if James Wiseman is not waived by Saturday. However, despite a mandate to remain under the second apron, New York is allowed to keep Wiseman and Bruce Brown to start the season.

The deadline for rookie extensions is Monday by 6 p.m. ET.

Since the start of the offseason, five players -- Victor Wembanyama, Amen and Ausar Thompson, Keyonte George and Brandin Podziemski -- have signed rookie extensions. The 2023 rookie class of extended players are below the per year average of 11 players we have seen since 2023.

Some of the notable names to watch include Brandon Miller and Cason Wallace. Keep in mind that out of the 34 players who signed rookie extensions in the prior three seasons, 17 came on the last day of eligibility.

The rookie extension deadline is not the only date teams are paying attention to, however. Oct. 19 is also the deadline to extend veterans who have two years left on their contract -- not including an option year -- and the last day to reduce rosters to 15 players on standard contracts. -- Bobby Marks

"In a city like this, it's a blessing. I'm thankful for it, I don't take it for granted and I'm trying to make the most out of it." -- Eric Woodyard
