The Charlotte Hornets are waiving guard Rob Dillingham, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Dillingham was traded from the Chicago Bulls on Saturday for Buddy Hield and cash. The Hornets created a $9.6 million trade exception with the move.

Dillingham, 21, appeared in 30 games for the Bulls last season, averaging 9.6 points and 2.8 assists.

SGA on chance at historic third straight MVP

At Oklahoma City Thunder media day, guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander discussed the possibility of winning a third straight NBA MVP award and whether that's something he ponders going into this season.

"No different than any other year: Try to be the best player I can be, try to implement the things I just worked on," Gilgeous-Alexander said.

"The decision for MVP is literally 82 games away. I'm not going to win the award in the first week of the season. ... That kind of recipe for me in the past has kind of worked, and I've been fortunate to win two in a row.

"We need to be laser focused on ourselves. We need to take the lessons from that [Western Conference finals] series, for sure, and we did. But it's certainly not something that we overcorrect for, because you end up chasing your shadow, and it prevents you from being your best as you move forward."

ESPN's Summer Forecast gave Gilgeous-Alexander the fourth-best chance at the 2027 MVP, behind Victor Wembanyama, Nikola Jokic and Luka Doncic. No player has won three consecutive MVPs since Larry Bird in 1984, 1985 and 1986. -- Baxter Holmes

Doncic talks LeBron exit, Lakers "championship" ceiling
Speaking to ESPN's Brian Windhorst during Los Angeles Lakers media day, guard Luka Doncic detailed his reaction to LeBron James leaving for the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer and why he thinks a successful 2026-27 includes a Lakers run to the title:

"It was kind of sad. Playing with LeBron was amazing. There's a lot of things I learned from him. ... We all know who LeBron James is."

Shams: Duren's relationship with Pistons "has fractures"

Simmons "didn't touch a ball for a year"

During Sacramento Kings media day, guard Ben Simmons laid out the reasons he chose the Kings and why he's excited for the 2026-27 season.

"The expectations are low. I feel like that's been something on me too, so we can relate in that way," Simmons told reporters. "I think we have a chip on our shoulder."

Simmons last played in 2024-25, appearing in 51 games for the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers. The three-time All-Star said the time away gave him the chance to focus on "getting my body right and my mind right."

Pistons GM hasn't spoken with Duren all summer

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons have a decision to make as the clock ticks closer to Oct. 1 -- the deadline to sign a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer.

For Duren, he can accept the five-year, $200 million contract that has been offered by Detroit or he can become the first player named All-NBA or All-Star to sign the qualifying offer. If he chooses the latter, Duren will hold veto power on any trade this season and be an unrestricted free agent next summer.

For the Pistons, weighing the risk of having an All-NBA player on a one-year contract and, more importantly, the likelihood he will depart next summer as a free agent is key.

There are eight projected teams that have significant cap space to sign Duren to a four-year, $189 million max contract.

"I can't control the different things that he does or his group does," Pistons president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon said at media day. "For me, it's control what we can and letting him know he is a big part of what we do."

Langdon also said he hasn't spoken with Duren all summer during Pistons media day. -- Bobby Marks

Mitchell: LeBron to Cavs made sense "for a lot of reasons"

At Cavaliers media day, Donovan Mitchell said that in his mind, he thought LeBron James would return to Cleveland because "for a lot of reasons it made sense."

"I didn't think Philly. I thought if he didn't come here, it'd be Golden State," Mitchell said.

After being swept in the Eastern Conference finals by the eventual champion New York Knicks then missing out on James in free agency, Cleveland kept its core intact. The Cavs signed Mitchell to a four-year, $273 million maximum extension and re-signed James Harden to a three-year, $97 million contract. Cleveland did make one major addition by acquiring Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets in a multiteam trade then signing the restricted free agent to a four-year, $88 million deal.

Speaking for the first time since their extensions, Mitchell and Harden both said their approaches to their new deals -- Mitchell signing as soon as he was eligible with Harden opting out to give Cleveland more flexibility to make moves -- reflected a team-first mindset.

"This is something that I want to do, and I want to win a championship," Harden said. "So, what does that look like? Making the team better, making the team whole to where we give ourselves a chance. By the way, you can have the best talented team, which I've been on before, and still not win.

"We waited, waited, waited until the front office called me, made sure that we got everything that we can get, and then we signed. We got a long way to go, but I love the direction and steps that we're taking here as a unit from top to bottom." -- Daniel Oyefusi

MacMahon: Thunder adjusting to roster changes
The departures of three championship-winning teammates doesn't yet feel like reality for Thunder superstar Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who kidded that he still expected Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to show up for Oklahoma City's team picture Monday afternoon.

"It's the business of the NBA, right?" Gilgeous-Alexander said, referring to the series of financially motivated trades. "I don't think anybody has played with all 12 guys their whole career. It sucks a little bit.

"My mind never even went to what we were going to be like on the court. It was more like the brotherhood."

As fellow OKC guard Jalen Williams added, "It's the weirdest thing ever." -- Tim MacMahon

Clippers announce Ingram has partially torn Achilles

The LA Clippers announced they found a partially torn Achilles tendon in Brandon Ingram's foot after his recent heel surgery. He will miss the start of the 2026-27 season.

Jokic: "I'm gonna sign next year"

Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic reiterated his commitment to the franchise at Monday's media day.

"I'm gonna sign next year," Jokic said. "If they want me."

Curry said knee is ready to go for the season

Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry addressed the media Monday in offering positive updates on his injured knee.

"Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues," Curry said. "I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with."

Curry did acknowledge a "management element" but said there are currently no restrictions.

Nuggets confident in Jokic's future with franchise

Members of the Denver Nuggets' front office, general manager Jon Wallace and executive vice president of basketball Ben Tenzer addressed the media on Monday and answered questions regarding Nikola Jokic's future with the franchise. The three-time MVP didn't sign an extension this offseason.

"We feel very comfortable with the relation and trust there," Tenzer said. "We have no concerns."

LeBron: I wanted to finish my career with the Knicks
New Philadelphia 76er LeBron James said his decision came down to five teams this offseason and that he envisioned going to the New York Knicks before they won the 2026 title.

"I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden," James told ESPN on Monday during the 76ers' media day. "One of the best places I've ever played.

"I think it's the No. 1 arena in the world, as far as for a basketball player. But after they beat San Antonio, I was like, 'Hey, I can't.' I couldn't do it."

James and the 76ers will play the Knicks at the Garden on opening night, Oct. 20.

No update on Gary Trent Jr. investigation

Milwaukee Bucks governor Wes Edens did not provide an update on the league investigation into Gary Trent Jr.'s contract.

"I don't have any update," Edens said. "We're working with the league and fully cooperating with them. But I don't have any insight beyond that."

The NBA is looking into a potential cap-circumvention violation by the Bucks around Trent's deal this offseason.

Cronin: Blazers have "belief" in Ja Morant
Portland Trail Blazers' general manager Joe Cronin addressed why the franchise decided to trade for Ja Morant this offseason during Portland's media day on Monday.

"Just straight belief in Ja," Cronin said. "Our view of Ja as still a very high-level player.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit, but we're very focused on talent."

Cronin also said veteran guard Jrue Holiday could play some minutes on the wing for Portland this season, while adding that Holiday and veteran guard Damian Lillard will have a positive influence on Morant.

Kerr: Rookie Lendeborg going to "play a ton"

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said during Monday's media day that he expects rookie Yaxel Lendeborg to "play a ton" this season.

"He's clearly going to play a ton," Kerr said. "He gives us the size and the versatility that we need.

"Whether he's a starter or coming off the bench, that will be determined the next couple of weeks."

Lendeborg was the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft and averaged 15.1 points per game at Michigan last season.

Embiid: 'Extremely excited' about this year's team
Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid said Monday that he feels like the team finally has the right mix of players, after an offseason in which the franchise traded for Jaylen Brown and signed LeBron James to join the young guard tandem of VJ Edgecombe and Tyrese Maxey.

"It's hard to win when you get a group of guys together for one year, two years, maybe," he said. "I'm extremely excited about this team because we have the right mix of veteran leadership and younger guys. We might have some ups and downs, but we're gonna get there."

Wembanyama addresses last year's Finals loss
After leading by double digits in each of the five games in last season's NBA Finals, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama said his memories of it will fuel the team this season.

"I couldn't imagine a better motivation," he said.

Harper addresses role for coming season
After offseason chatter about his role, San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper said he'd follow the coaches' lead this season.

"Everyone has a competitive edge to them. But the biggest thing for me is whatever I can do, just like last year, to help the team win," he said. "Whatever position the coaches think is best for me to be in, that's the position I'll happily go in."

First look at LeBron in a 76ers uniform
New Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James is taking questions from reporters on Monday. Here's what he had to say when asked about his initial impressions of his team:

"Everybody is on the same page," James said. "We are all speaking the same language."

LeBron addressed his role too, saying he's open to whatever the team needs from him to win.

"Whatever they need me to do," he said. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything. ... Literally, I can do everything"

Kawhi: I was a distraction, ready to move forward
In his first public appearance with the Toronto Raptors after a controversy-filled summer, Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA's investigation into him and his business dealings.

"I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation. But in talking with the NBA and PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor," he said. "I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates or do any of that stuff, minicamp stuff, so, moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors."

Haliburton: I am 100% healthy
Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton said Monday that he is healthy and ready for the season.

"I am healthy. I am 100%," he said. "There will be no restrictions. That is not news. There is no source. I am the source. I am ready to go for the year."

Porzingis out indefinitely in blow to Warriors
Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis is out indefinitely to open training camp with a health issue, according to the team.
In late July, Porzingis agreed to a two-year, $40 million contract with a player option on the second season to return to the Warriors.

Brown: KAT, Hart extension talks won't be a distraction
After reports surfaced last week that negotiations between the New York Knicks and center Karl-Anthony Towns had hit a stalemate, coach Mike Brown said Monday neither Towns' situation nor Hart's would linger in the locker room.

"We talk about everything [with the team]," Brown said. "We don't want to have any elephants in the room."

"I'm not involved in it. They'll figure it out. Control what you can control."

And here's what Towns said about a potential extension: "I've made it known I want to play here. Been a fan since I was a kid. I'd like to get it done."

Hornets GM: Brandon Miller to be ready for training camp
After undergoing offseason surgery on his left shoulder, Hornets wing Brandon Miller should be a full participant in training camp and "ready to roll" for opening night, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Monday.

Miller, 23, is entering his fourth NBA season after being the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft.

Duren won't be at Pistons media day, start of camp
Detroit Pistons All-Star center Jalen Duren is not attending the team's media day on Monday or the start of training camp as his contract standoff continues, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Monday.

Duren, a restricted free agent, is declining the team's five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer as both sides remain at a stalemate ahead of the Thursday deadline on a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, sources said.

Sept. 26

Bulls trade Dillingham to Hornets for Hield, cash
The Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets agreed to a trade sending Rob Dillingham to Charlotte for Buddy Hield and cash, the teams announced Saturday.

2026 NBA offseason trade grades

Sept. 25

What's next for Curry and the Warriors?
Stephen Curry's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings.

The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in position to have extra spending power next summer.

By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A

Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury
The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury.

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

Grizzlies waive Russell
The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

stories.body:
Paris Saint-Germain winger Désiré Doué has caught the eye of some top Premier League clubs, while Juventus have made Monaco and USMNT striker Folarin Balogun their top priority for the January transfer window. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Arsenal, Chelsea and Manchester City are monitoring Paris Saint-Germain winger Désiré Doué, alongside Bayern Munich, according to TEAMtalk. However, all the suitors face a setback in their hopes to sign him as PSG are progressing in talks over a contract extension with the 21-year-old France international to secure his future beyond 2029.

- Juventus have made Monaco striker Folarin Balogun their top priority for the January transfer window due to technical and financial factors, reports Tuttosport. The 25-year-old USMNT international is expected to leave Monaco after a €40 million summer move to Everton collapsed, while Atlético Madrid's Alexander Sørloth and Frosinone loanee Antonio Raimondo remain alternative targets for Juve.

- Chelsea have focused their attention on signing AFC Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott following their failed summer attempt, Florian Plettenberg reports. Liverpool are also looking to reunite Scott with Andoni Iraola, while TEAMtalk suggests the Cherries are targeting AZ Alkmaar's Kees Smit and Lazio's Kenneth Taylor as potential replacements for the 23-year-old England international.

- Chelsea, AC Milan, Galatasaray and Fenerbahçe are most keen on landing Brighton & Hove Albion midfielder Yasin Ayari, per TEAMtalk. Ayari, 23, has a deal that expires in the summer, though Brighton hold a one-year option to extend it which has created uncertainty around his future. The Sweden international has also been linked with Newcastle United, Arsenal, Manchester United, Liverpool, Atlético Madrid, Borussia Dortmund, Roma and Juventus.

- Former Manchester United winger Jadon Sancho has turned down an offer from Getafe after receiving a lucrative proposal from Saudi Arabia, according to Marca. The 26-year-old is a free agent and had requested a net salary of €3 million through the end of the season, which exceeded Getafe's financial capabilities.

- Chelsea, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United all sent scouts to watch Club Brugge striker Nicolò Tresoldi score a hat-trick against Sint-Truiden. (TEAMtalk)

- Bayern Munich are monitoring Newcastle United loanee Nick Woltemade at Juventus as they evaluate a backup for Harry Kane. (Gazzetta dello Sport)

- Barcelona, Napoli, and Juventus are tracking Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Lucas Bergvall amid his limited first-team minutes this season. (TEAMtalk)

- Manchester United have shifted their January transfer priorities toward reinforcing their defensive unit. (Football Insider)

- Brighton & Hove Albion and RB Leipzig could make a January bid to sign Juventus winger Adin Licina, who is currently impressing on loan at Cremonese. (Tuttosport)

- Lecce are preparing for defender Tiago Gabriel to depart in January amidst growing interest from Everton. (Football Insider)

- Leeds United are targeting a cut-price January deal to sign Porto left back Zaidu Sanusi. (Football Insider)

- Right-back João Mário could seek a January exit from Fiorentina to secure greater playing time. (Nicolò Schira)

stories.headline: 'They smoke us': Why a moon astronaut thinks F1 is ahead of NASA
stories.summary: Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman explains to ESPN why F1's engineering is ahead of NASA's, his admiration for Mercedes and what he learned on the moon.
stories.body:
Somewhere between Earth and the moon, Reid Wiseman encountered a problem. The windows of his Artemis II spacecraft were filthy.

It wasn't a mechanical failure, the haunting bleep of a master alarm or some other unforeseen consequence borne out of attempting to travel further than any human beings in history. Instead, the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission had spent so much time with their faces pressed against the glass, gazing in awe at both the diminishing Earth in one direction and the extraordinary lunar landscape growing bigger in the other, that the windows were covered in smudges.

"We were looking out at Earth and we were looking out at the moon all the time," Wiseman told ESPN. "Victor [Glover], my pilot, made a comment when we got into our first orbit of Earth, he's like, 'that's the last time Reid ever looked inside [the spacecraft].'

- Nate Saunders on the contradictions of Austin's COTA

- How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

- Fernando Alonso slams 'low quality bottom third of the grid'

"We had to do a photo analysis of the windows so that the geology team could make sure there was no damage, or if they were seeing blemishes on lunar photography, they could relay it back. And I was looking at the windows before I got the camera out to do the survey, and I called down to Mission Control and said, 'hey, first, I need to clean them, because the amount of grease marks from our noses and foreheads on the windows, it was just completely covered.'"

For the commander of the first crewed mission to the moon in more than half a century, it was an understandable distraction. The view was unlike anything he had experienced before, even during his previous six-month stint aboard the International Space Station.

"We're human. Making sure the spacecraft is operating is of the prime of importance. But right underneath that is absorbing the experience. The thing that struck me most looking at the Earth is it got very small, and then it got, like, that big," Wiseman said, pushing his thumb and index finger almost completely together.

"But really looking at the moon was the three-dimensionality of everything. You're not looking through an atmosphere. Everything is crystal clear, everything. The blacks, the craters, the bumps, the sun hitting the crater rim, it was profoundly crystal clear, and all four of us felt that exact same thing. Your brain was having trouble processing the clarity with which we were seeing this three-dimensional moon right there out of the window."

Spine-tingling stuff, even if here it was slightly off-topic, at least in an official capacity.

The premise of Wiseman's interview time with ESPN was not primarily about space. Although when you're talking to someone who has travelled a quarter of a million miles from Earth, how could it be about anything else?

Sitting at Austin's Circuit of the Americas, Wiseman was not wearing the orange spacesuit of Artemis II, nor the familiar dark blue of NASA, but the white of Mercedes' Formula 1 team's team kit. Six months after returning from his historic journey around the moon, Wiseman became an ambassador for the German manufacturer. Last year, he and his daughter had attended the United States Grand Prix on general admission tickets. Then, for all intents and purposes, Wiseman was just another person baking in the Texas sun with thousands of other people. Returning a year later he can boast that he's one of just nine living humans to have seen the far side of the moon with their own eyes.

The setting of the interview prompted an obvious question.

How does NASA compare to Formula 1? The answer was surprising.

"Oh, they crush us," he replied. "I mean, the level of engineering here, they smoke us."

Wiseman's view is rooted in the priorities of the two disciplines. NASA places a premium on proven technology and backup systems, even if that means carrying additional weight into space to ensure the mission objectives are met. Formula 1, meanwhile, is about the relentless pursuit of performance and pushing the boundaries of engineering in search of even the smallest advantage. As we spoke, we were surrounded by Mercedes' race operation -- engineers, mechanics, media team, performance coaches, who have impressed him as much as the technology.

"In spaceflight, what we really need is tried and true, redundancy, and we can accept a little bit of a mass penalty," he said. "Here, they're just pushing everything to the next level, and just every single thing is ... it's not just the cars, it's the humans. You know, everybody's walking around with WHOOP straps, and monitoring everything about themselves. They're all basically athletes. They're all going all in at all times. I love the way they deal with human performance and mechanical performance."

The competition aspect of Formula 1 -- which pits Mercedes against 10 other teams every race -- is always going to skew a comparison between Antonelli's world and Wiseman's world. For the Artemis II commander, it's the hunger to win that sets Formula 1 apart.

"At the end of the day in our work, there's a really large team of experts that sit just under the fanfare, but are the ones that are the true heroes that have the real courage. And then on top are these people who are willing to push the envelope a little bit and go.

"What is a little different for us is I have a crew of four people that are together in the spacecraft and working to try to make this mission the best it can be. In these cars, it is George [Russell] going all in, killer instinct ... Kimi [Antonelli] going all in, killer instinct. Occasionally they might meet in a corner and then I'm like, 'oh dear god, let's get through the corner.'"

For Mercedes, that focus on performance has seen the German team climb back to the pinnacle of the sport this year. Wiseman was speaking ahead of a U.S. Grand Prix which saw Kimi Antonelli move to the verge of becoming the sport's youngest-ever world champion at 20 years old.

This weekend, he will almost certainly wrap it up in Mexico City.

Wiseman can remember his interaction with Antonelli in 2024, before he had even started racing in Formula 1. Even then, Wiseman could see traits that have helped propel Antonelli to the brink of history.

"I met Kimi briefly when he was touring the Johnson Space Centre, and he invited me to a race when he was there," Wiseman said.

"[He was] 17. When I met him, the first thing I thought was how astonishingly humble and down to earth he was. But at the same time, he's a little goofy, which I love, but he's just curious about everything. We were touring with a few other drivers, but Kimi was asking every question about every single thing, whether he needed the information or not. Those are the people I try to latch on to because that curiosity is so powerful.

"You walk around, why is that cloud there? Why is that bird flying? How is it doing that? Why are these tyres better than these tyres?"

Antonelli's rise came after a rollercoaster rookie season in 2025. The young Italian has this year made a lot of the support network Mercedes put around him - team boss Toto Wolff's arm-over-the-shoulder approach to some of Antonelli's early mistakes were key. So has been the oversight of his race engineer, Peter Bonnington, who brought with him the experience of working in the same role with Lewis Hamilton.

Even here, Wiseman cannot help but point to where the two worlds overlap in some way.

"I chuckle at the way Bono and Kimi talk [on the radio]. It feels exactly like us in space, where we'll say something to the engineering team, and then when we unkey the mic, the engineering team will be like, 'they don't know what they're talking about', and then they'll come up with an answer for us, and they'll send it back. I love hearing that.

"I love it when the engineers and the drivers joke around on the radio, and you can just tell. It's just a great relationship."

Wiseman's link-up with Mercedes is a unique thing, but he feels right at home. He admits he was never one of those "crazy space kids" who could name every Apollo astronaut or had Neil Armstrong as a boyhood hero. But there was an interest in racing from a young age. He grew up going to NASCAR races with his father in Delaware, although they never did fulfill their dream of watching an Indy 500 together. His first chance to see Formula 1 in person was in 2023, invited by McLaren and Mercedes.

Wiseman admits he initially wondered what to expect from the "terrifying Toto Wolff," but has since come to admire the culture the Mercedes boss has established.

"What really struck me was, he's actually not scary, he's hilarious in his own humour. What I noticed as we were here, if you look around this place, there's no flash, it's just professionalism. 'We were going to go get the job done, and not just on the track.' It's the way they take care of the fans, the way they take care of the sponsors, the way they take care of the engineering team."

As he continued, Wiseman gestured over to Mercedes reserve driver Fred Vesti for another anecdote. "I went out for a run this morning with the engineers and did a swim down in Austin with them, and then I couldn't keep up on the way home, so I ran with Fred Vesti. He hung back and ran with me. The culture here always comes from the top. You can just tell Toto has one hell of a racing team that also knows how to take care of people."

Here is where he thinks NASA can learn a great deal from Formula 1's super-active team members. "Astronauts have to put a pretty good premium on our own health and physical conditioning, because we're going to be weightless, and our bones and our muscles are going to waste during the mission.

"So we put a big premium on that. We don't put as big of a premium on our support team and making sure they are at their highest level, and I think we can raise their level of expertise. They spend a lot of their days sitting in chairs, analysing data, and most of them would probably be upset if I said, let's go run three miles, but I think we can elevate the human performance, and we should really look at that. Because you look around in this team, everybody is fit, they're hungry, they're getting after it, and I think we can elevate the team [at NASA]."

Wiseman was brought to Mercedes to tell these kinds of stories. His role is to work with team partners, sponsors and guests to explain the overlap between the two worlds and, of course, to tell captivating stories about his own experiences. It's easy to see what he brings to the table. Had our interview not already overrun its 15-minute slot, it would have been easy to have kept going and going. "Toto likes the way I communicate," he said. "I think [guests] also like hearing stories of four humans that have gone further from Earth than anyone else. And I think there's just a lot of good storytelling and a sense of adventure that comes from that."

Inevitably, of course, our conversation drifted back to space.

Wiseman's anecdotes do not end with the stories he can tell verbally. At one point, he reached for his phone to show a picture with legendary Apollo-era flight director Gene Kranz, now 91, and Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise, taken earlier that week. Scattered through his camera roll were photographs he had taken himself of the moon from inside the spacecraft, through those smudged windows. Not a bad collection of snaps to have at your fingertips.

The Artemis II mission captivated a worldwide audience. In one of its most poignant moments, Wiseman's crewmates surprised him by naming a lunar crater in honour of his late wife, Carroll. But while millions of people followed their every move from Earth, the four astronauts were experiencing something rather different.

It is only since returning home that Wiseman has begun to appreciate just how much the mission meant to those watching.

"One thing that has been so rewarding is fame is not really that fun. I don't know how Kimi and George deal with that," he said. "But I was at an airport over in Europe the other day, and a dad came over to me and said, 'Hey, my daughter thinks you're Reid Wiseman. Are you?' And I said, yes, I am.

"And he turns to her, and this 10-year-old girl from the Philippines comes running over and just gave me the biggest hug. She knew everything about Christina, everything about Victor, everything about Jeremy.

"And I took this little medallion off my backpack and gave it to her, and she was so emotional. That stuff just is, it's all we could have ever wished for."

It was one of countless stories Wiseman and his crewmates have been hearing since they returned, providing a new perspective on a journey they are still coming to terms with themselves.

"We were all together three weeks ago. And we hadn't been together in a few weeks, and we were like, how's everything going? What are you feeling right now?

"And we all have this common feeling of we're starting to understand that we experienced this mission, but Earth experienced it. And now we're loving hearing the stories.

"Now that we've kind of processed the mission, we're listening to the stories from our friends at launch, when Carroll Crater was named, the amount of emotion that was involved in that. People were waking up and turning on the YouTube channel to see where are they today, what's going on.

"And we realised we went on a mission, but actually Earth kind of did too."

stories.headline: Salkilld, Saint Denis to headline UFC Fight Night in Sydney
stories.summary: West Australian Quillan Salkilld will headline a UFC Fight Night lightweight matchup with Benoît Saint Denis in Sydney in February.
stories.body:
West Australian Quillan Salkilld will return to the Octagon in Sydney, after it was confirmed he'll headline the UFC Fight Night with a lightweight bout against Frenchman Benoît Saint Denis on February 7 (AEDT).

Salkilld, 26, is a former Australian rules footballer who turned to MMA after leaving school at 16, and boasts an impressive 13-1 professional record (6-0 in UFC) with five 'performance of the night' bonuses.

The Broome native has won four consecutive fights with a first-round finish, most recently submitting Mateusz Gamrot in their UFC Fight Night clash in Perth in August. He's widely regarded as Australia's next big combat star.

Meanwhile Saint Denis, 30, is one of the lightweight division's most dangerous finishers, and has a 17-4 professional record.

Peter Kloczko, senior vice president of UFC Australia and New Zealand, said the Fight Night -- to take place at Sydney's Afterpay Arena -- would be an "unforgettable event" featuring one of Australia's brightest young stars.

"UFC Fight Night Sydney is set to be another huge moment for Australian fans, and Quillan Salkilld versus Benoît Saint Denis is a main event that delivers everything we look for in this sport," he said in the official release.

"Quillan has been one of the breakout stars of the UFC's lightweight division, while Benoît is one of the most dangerous and exciting finishers in the sport. Bringing this fight to Sydney will make for an unforgettable night."

Further fights on the card will be released in due course.

7:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | WSH -238, O/U: 6.5

In the final season of Alex Ovechkin's record-breaking NHL career, he gets to play against all of his Metro Division rivals four times each. This will be the first showdown against the Flyers.

Ovechkin has 54 goals and 32 assists in 82 career regular-season games against Philly, including two tallies in the most recent matchup on March 31.

The two teams split their season series in 2025-26, and the Flyers would appear to need the two points quite a bit more given their lackluster start.

Calgary Flames at Edmonton Oilers

8:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | EDM -218, O/U: 6.5

No matter the players involved, there is always a little extra juice when the NHL's two Alberta-based teams square off. That's no different this season, despite the fact that the Flames haven't made the postseason since 2022 -- when the Oilers knocked them out in five games in the second round.

This will be the first matchup between the clubs this season, and it will (likely) feature the NHL's second star of the week, Devin Cooley, in goal for the Flames.

On the other side, the Oilers have the NHL's first star of the week, Leon Draisaitl, who hopes to get the upper hand in this matchup. He'll have help; while Drasaitl is second in the NHL in scoring this season (24 points through 12 games), teammate Connor McDavid is first with 34 points.

New Jersey Devils at Colorado Avalanche

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -192, O/U: 6.5

Just 25 hours after opening puck drop against the Central Division powerhouse Dallas Stars, the Devils will face off against the Central Division powerhouse Colorado Avalanche.

In the teams' first matchup this season, the Devils took a 3-1 lead early in the third period, and Jesper Boqvist made it 4-1 with an empty-netter at 16:05. The Avs got two back -- both scored by Artturi Lehkonen -- but couldn't find the equalizer.

Will Wednesday's game provide us another exciting finish?

Toronto Maple Leafs at Seattle Kraken

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -115, O/U: 6.5

It's still quite early in the season, but both of these teams enter this contest in playoff positions in their respective divisions after missing out on the postseason fun in 2026.

The Leafs will hope they get an effort like the one they had Saturday in Edmonton (a 7-2 win) as opposed to Monday in Calgary (a 5-2 loss). Seattle has also had some inconsistent results as of late, with wins over the Mammoth and Red Wings sandwiched between blowout losses to the Panthers and Wild.

stories.headline: Who I would -- and would not -- want to be this AFL offseason
stories.summary: The AFL offseason is in full swing but it won't stop us from analysing the landscape. Here's who Jake Michaels would (and wouldn't!) want to be heading into 2027.
stories.body:
From Brisbane's stunning three-peat to Fremantle's Grand Final capitulation, high-profile free agent signings to ongoing legal battles, so much has happened in the AFL world over the past month. So, who would you want to be (and not want to be) this off-season.

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Those I WOULD NOT want to be this AFL offseason
Ross Lyon
No coach will enter season 2027 under more scrutiny and pressure than Ross Lyon. St Kilda was widely tipped to rise up the ladder this season just gone after being the most active club during the previous trade and free agency period. Instead, the Saints severely underwhelmed, winning just 10 games and finishing a disappointing 11th on the ladder, 10 premiership points outside of the wildcard finals. The club is desperate to retain the services of superstar midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who is out of contract at season's end and could easily be tempted with a blockbuster move back to South Australia. As a result, St Kilda's powerbrokers likely won't tolerate another sluggish start, which means Lyon has absolutely zero margin for error in 2027.

Fremantle fans
Alright, alright, I'm sorry to bring it up again. And please feel free to skip ahead if you don't want to re-live it once more. But the reality is every single Dockers fan will be replaying those harrowing final four-and-a-bit minutes of the Grand Final in their mind all offseason, wondering how on earth their team coughed up what appeared to be an insurmountable late lead. The heartbreaking loss to Brisbane is as devastating as it gets for a footy club and you could almost understand if any Fremantle fan never wanted to watch the sport again. Seriously, I'm not sure how you ever get over that loss. It all just means the next five months are going to feel like an eternity.

Andrew McGrath
It was an incredibly disappointing season from new Essendon skipper Andrew McGrath, who averaged a career-low in disposals, kicked just two goals, and failed to poll a single Brownlow Medal vote. To be a captain of a club that won just two games for the entire year and still be unable to crack the top 10 of the best and fairest count is pretty embarrassing, really. With former skipper Zach Merrett now no longer at the club, McGrath, who has now been in the league for a decade and tallied 200 games, is Essendon's main man. It's time he starts to play like it or else he risks further damage to his reputation.

Chris Fagan's replacement
Whoever is entrusted with the task of succeeding Chris Fagan at the Lions will be feeling the pressure and the eyes of the footy world on them from day one. It's a bit like following Jerry Seinfeld on stage. How can you possibly back up that act!? Fagan completely revitalised Brisbane, leading the club out of the doldrums and to its second three-peat this century. And while Fagan's tenure is up and dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale has departed for Collingwood, nobody feels as if the Lions are over the hump. In fact, quite the contrary. The age profile of this list should have them contending for years to come. That can be both a blessing or a curse for any new coach.

The Pullman Five

Okay, this one might be a tad on the nose, but who would want to be one of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice, or James Jordan this offseason? The incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne on the eve of finals remains a legal matter, meaning there are still so many unknowns when it comes to the footballing careers of these five. Can Heeney and Warner ever ingratiate themselves to the Swans' faithful once more? Will Bice and Jordan be shuffled out of the best team? And then there's Blakey. North Melbourne gave up the farm for his signature and much will be expected of him at his new club. I'm just not sure he's the difference maker they think he is.

An (existing and competing) expansion club
At what point do we stop referring to Gold Coast and GWS as expansion clubs? Probably now. But I'm lumping them together in here for different reasons. The Suns were a total shambles this year, falling from flag favourite after three rounds to finishing in the bottom six and winning just two games after the mid-season byes. Spearhead Ben King has now departed the club and rumour has it Matt Rowell wants to follow suit. Damien Hardwick is under the pump and must show something in year four at the helm. Meanwhile, the Giants just held a fire sale, clearing out Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs. It's a bold move, and while it could pay dividends down the track, you figure there simply has to be some short term pain.

Those I WOULD want to be this AFL offseason
Zach Merrett
This time last year Merrett would have been top of my other list, but the veteran midfielder's wish of a fresh start at a new club has now been granted, and that must feel like an enormous weight has been lifted from his shoulders. Merrett joins the Hawks, a club which could easily have won the premiership this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's late heroics during preliminary final weekend. It means that for the first time in Merrett's career he will enter a season truly believing his side can go all the way. That's got to be a great feeling for an elite player who has toiled away for so long and enjoyed little success.

Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera
As we've established, his coach might be under immense pressure, but Wanganeen-Milera certainly shouldn't be feeling the pinch. In fact, he goes into next season with all options and possibilities on the table. If the Saints turn out to make good on their promise from last year and actually show they can compete with those at the pointy end, then he may well elect to sign on and remain at the club. But if 2027 turns out to be more of the same, he will have his choice of 17 new destinations to call home, including the two clubs from his home state of South Australia. Make no mistake, Wanganeen-Milera will be both the most discussed and in-demand player in the sport next season.

Andrew Mackie and Geelong's entire recruitment staff
When the siren sounded on the trade and free agency period, Geelong list boss Andrew Mackie should have been pumping his fists and popping bottles of champagne in celebration. The Cats have been arguably the biggest winners of the offseason to date, improving across every line with additions of former Giants captain Toby Greene, reliable ruck Rowan Marshall, and still criminally underrated key defender Jordan Ridley. It's a hefty haul and a great salvage after the club discovered at the eleventh hour it would be missing out on the services of Zak Butters. Mackie and his team have done their job, now it's over to Chris Scott and the playing group.

Fremantle fans
Alright, so there are the obvious reasons why you wouldn't want to be a Fremantle fan this offseason, but there are also plenty of reasons why you absolutely would. The Dockers came within an inch of winning their first premiership last month and proved to the footy world, and their supporters, the club has a list to not only go all the way in 2027 but remain one of the premier sides in the league for the next half decade. Just about everyone on this Fremantle squad is yet to hit their prime and has serious scope to improve next year. That should be both a worrying thought for the other 17 clubs and a great comfort to those who cheer for the men in purple.

Jason Horne-Francis
The departure of superstar midfielder Zak Butters during free agency means the keys to Port Adelaide now firmly belong to Horne-Francis. Some might argue he's shared those keys with Butters in recent years, but there's simply no denying who will be top dog at Port heading into next season. Horne-Francis is still just 23 years of age but he has shown he possesses all of the attributes to succeed as his club's main man. I expect him to relish the extra responsibility, too, and take his game to even greater heights. Jason, train hard and we'll see you in 2027!

Jaymie Graham
It must feel pretty special knowing a club made the decision to part ways with a four-time premiership-winning coach in favour of you, despite the fact you've never coached a senior AFL game. Graham arrives at Arden Street with an impressive resume as an assistant and has been tasked with ending North Melbourne's decade-long finals drought. Some will make the case he faces similar pressure to whoever takes over from Fagan at the Lions, but I see his role, at least in the immediate future, as one which carries far less of a burden. Given North's recent struggles, he will be offered (a little) time to get things right. His team is also in the sweet spot of being enough to win with now but not good enough to carry crazy expectation.

stories.headline: Kane's long road to Ballon d'Or glory ends with his crowning moment
stories.summary: After a remarkable year for Bayern Munich and England, Harry Kane becoming the world's best player is the ultimate reward for years of perseverance.
stories.body:
LONDON -- It is nine years since Harry Kane lingered at the back of the London Palladium at the end of a soccer awards show.

The Best FIFA Football Awards in 2017 had just concluded with Cristiano Ronaldo handed the men's top prize in addition to leading a team of the year including Lionel Messi, Neymar, Sergio Ramos and Gianluigi Buffon.

As the audience filed out and a few mere mortals loitered in the hope of a selfie, Kane stood near the exit, casting a longing stare at the winners on stage. He has dreamed all his life of being in their place, considered in the same breath as the game's greats.

On Monday, at the same storied West End venue, about nine miles from his birthplace in Leytonstone, he finally is. Sat next to Lamine Yamal with last year's winner Rodri one place further away, Kane kept company with the elite. And then he joined them.

Last week in Munich, he told reporters he had found the wait to learn the winner "very stressful" for himself and his family. The final few hours on Monday won't have helped. The rain present earlier in the day subsided, but the controversy did not.

Less than three hours before the ceremony was due to start, the official website published a profile of Kane as the 2026 Ballon d'Or winner. Alongside one for Kylian Mbappé and one for Yamal. They were swiftly deleted. The entire ceremony was then delayed by 45 minutes with no official reason given, amid some speculation that the notorious London traffic was responsible.

Kane won on the undercard -- the Gerd Müller Men's Award or the Striker of the Year -- to cheers from the locals in the audience. The raucous reaction from the cheap seats before addressing the crowd was a prelude to what followed. It was palpably welcome but not, by itself, an indication of the big one: Striker of the Year is not decided by vote but simply by goals, and Kane's 73 was the best in the men's game.

Having waited for over a decade to live this moment, a few extra minutes made no difference in the end.

"Wow, wow, wow," he said after taking the stage before thanking Tottenham Hotspur by saying "I wouldn't be where I am without you" in a moment of typical class.

Monday's Ballon d'Or triumph is the crowning moment for a player whose story of relentless professionalism and determined aspiration serves as an exemplar for any young player. British media is often criticized for prematurely building up players to an impossible level, only to then knock them down when that level is inevitably never reached.

Kane has always been a different case. He publicly judged himself against Ronaldo and Messi, two of the best in history, and used their devastating consistency as a target to match.

His numbers since joining Bayern Munich are staggering: 158 goals in 156 matches following a €120 million move from Tottenham in 2023. The Ballon d'Or voting period takes into account August 2025 to the end of the World Cup in July.

He scored 73 goals in 65 matches during that period, won the Bundesliga, the DFB-Pokal, the German Supercup and led England to their best FIFA World Cup finish in 60 years with third place, scoring six times at the tournament.

Back in 2017, "The Best" awards were a competition set up by FIFA as a rival to the Ballon d'Or after five years of partnership with organizers France Football had come to an end. Kane was on the 24-man shortlist for Best Men's Player that year. He finished 24th. Of course, his journey to the summit began much further back.

Coming through the Spurs academy, a young Kane had loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City, where you would find it extremely difficult to locate anyone honest who genuinely believed at the time they were in the presence of a future world-class talent. A nice kid, sure, a hard worker with a future in the game. But one of England's greatest?

Kane broke into Spurs' first team toward the end of the 2013-14 season and a year later was named PFA Young Player of the Year aged 21, making his England debut in the same season. He marked that moment against Lithuania with a goal then, too.

Fame was a novelty at this point. During a Tottenham preseason tour to Sydney, Kane innocently ventured out to a shopping center in his downtime. He was quickly mobbed by so many adoring fans that the club had to scramble a minibus to bring him back to the team hotel.

Kane went on to score 280 goals in 435 appearances for Spurs while breaking Wayne Rooney's all-time goal-scoring record for England. Barring injury, he will break Peter Shilton's appearance record of 125 caps next month, too.

There was, though, perhaps a sense in the buildup that Kane was not quite the global superstar his Ballon d'Or rivals were, most obviously Messi and Mbappé but also, despite his teenage years, Yamal, named Young Talent of the Year for the third consecutive year.

Former Spurs boss Jose Mourinho alluded to this in a conversation with Kane captured by Amazon in their "All or Nothing" series covering the 2019-20 campaign.

"The world looks to English football with an incredible respect but they still think that the movie stars of football belong to other places -- and I think we have to build also your status in that direction," he said.

Kane replied: "That's my aim. When you are at a club like Tottenham, of course we've done well, personally I've done well, but I want to be Ronaldo, Messi ..."

There he goes again. The Ballon d'Or is voted for by one journalist per country of FIFA's top 100 ranked nations, which brings a different dynamic than, say, the FIFA equivalent, which adds votes from national managers and captains.

He had never finished higher than 10th in the Ballon d'Or vote (2024). There are three criteria, listed in order of importance: individual performances, decisive and impressive character; collective performances and titles won; class and fair play.

And despite the Premier League being one of the United Kingdom's most successful global exports, English players have only ever won it five times (Sir Stanley Matthews, Sir Bobby Charlton and Kevin Keegan twice) and nobody has triumphed since Michael Owen in 2001.

That's more than two decades of unprecedented growth for the Premier League, and yet LaLiga often feels as though it is where the true individual talents reside. Players from Real Madrid and Barcelona have won it 12 times each. Manchester United are the most successful English club in Ballon d'Or history with four.

Kane, of course, left England in pursuit of silverware after a decade of personal achievement but collective frustration at Spurs. In doing so, he has ended up landing both silverware with Bayern and now the highest individual honor a player can attain.

"I am almost speechless," he said. "Being here in London has made it extra special. It made it a good omen for me tonight." Where once he stared at the Palladium stage, now all eyes are on him.
